claim: Influenza B virus causes a significant proportion of influenza-associated morbidity and mortality.
source: Influenza B causes a significant proportion of influenza-associated morbidity and mortality, and in some years is responsible for the major disease burden (Burnham et al., 2013; Paul Glezen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Burnham et al., 2013; Paul Glezen et al., 2013)

claim: Type A and B influenza viruses exhibit important differences in their ecology and evolution.
source: Although type A and B influenza viruses are closely related and have similarities in genome organization and protein structure (McCauley et al., 2012), they exhibit important differences in their ecology and evolution (Chen and Holmes, 2008; Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Chen and Holmes, 2008; Tan et al., 2013)

claim: Influenza B viruses were first recognized in 1940.
source: Influenza B viruses, first recognized in 1940, have circulated continuously in humans alongside influenza A viruses and are presumably derived from a single, as yet unknown, source (Francis, 1940; Chen and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Francis, 1940

claim: Influenza B viruses have circulated continuously in humans alongside influenza A viruses.
source: Influenza B viruses, first recognized in 1940, have circulated continuously in humans alongside influenza A viruses and are presumably derived from a single, as yet unknown, source (Francis, 1940; Chen and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Francis, 1940; Chen and Holmes, 2008)

claim: Influenza B infections are almost exclusively restricted to humans with only sporadic infections reported in wildlife.
source: Unlike influenza A viruses that can infect a wide range of species, influenza B infections are almost exclusively restricted to humans with only sporadic infections reported in wildlife (Osterhaus et al., 2000; Bodewes et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Osterhaus et al., 2000; Bodewes et al., 2013)

claim: The evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics of human influenza A H1N1 and H3N2 viruses have been well documented at the global scale.
source: While the evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics of human influenza A H1N1 and H3N2 viruses have been well documented at the global scale (Rambaut et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2008; Bedford et al., 2010; Bahl et al., 2011), the equivalent dynamics of the two influenza B virus lineages—B/Yamagata/16/88-like and B/Victoria/2/87-like, henceforth termed the Yamagata and Victoria viruses—are poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Rambaut et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2008; Bedford et al., 2010; Bahl et al., 2011)

claim: The equivalent dynamics of the two influenza B virus lineages are poorly understood.
source: While the evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics of human influenza A H1N1 and H3N2 viruses have been well documented at the global scale (Rambaut et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2008; Bedford et al., 2010; Bahl et al., 2011), the equivalent dynamics of the two influenza B virus lineages—B/Yamagata/16/88-like and B/Victoria/2/87-like, henceforth termed the Yamagata and Victoria viruses—are poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by the statement that dynamics are poorly understood, contrasting with well-documented A viruses

claim: Human influenza A H3N2 viruses exhibit limited genetic diversity at individual time-points due to periodic bottlenecks caused by strong selection in the hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) genes.
source: Human influenza A H3N2 viruses exhibit limited genetic diversity at individual time-points due to periodic bottlenecks caused by strong selection—known as 'antigenic drift'—in the hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) genes.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of H3N2 evolution

claim: H3N2 viruses exhibit an HA phylogenetic tree with a characteristic slender 'trunk' appearance.
source: This results in an HA phylogenetic tree with a characteristic slender 'trunk' (Fitch et al., 1997) appearance (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation (Fitch et al., 1997) and visual evidence in Figure 1A

claim: H3N2 viruses exhibit strong seasonal fluctuations in genetic diversity in temperate climate regions.
source: H3N2 viruses also exhibit strong seasonal fluctuations in genetic diversity in temperate climate regions (such as Australia and New Zealand) (Rambaut et al., 2008), mainly due to the local extinction of viral lineages at the end of each influenza season (Rambaut et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rambaut et al., 2008

claim: Seasonal H1N1 viruses exhibit short-term co-circulation of diverging virus populations.
source: A similar but weaker evolutionary pattern is observed in the seasonal H1N1 viruses that have circulated in humans for the majority of the previous century (1918–1957 and 1977–2009), with short-term co-circulation of diverging virus populations (Nelson et al., 2008b) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation (Nelson et al., 2008b) and visual evidence in Figure 1B

claim: Pandemic H1N1 (H1N1pdm09) viruses have exhibited only limited antigenic evolution since they emerged in 2009.
source: The pandemic H1N1 (H1N1pdm09) viruses have to date also only exhibited limited antigenic evolution since they emerged in 2009 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figure 1C

claim: Influenza B viruses are currently composed of two distinct lineages (Victoria and Yamagata) that diverged approximately 40 years ago.
source: In contrast, influenza B viruses are currently composed of two distinct lineages (Victoria and Yamagata) (Kanegae et al., 1990; Rota et al., 1990) (Figure 1D) that diverged approximately 40 years ago and which have since co-circulated on a global scale, despite frequent reassortment among them (Chen and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations (Kanegae et al., 1990; Rota et al., 1990; Chen and Holmes, 2008) and visual evidence in Figure 1D

claim: The Victoria and Yamagata lineages have co-circulated on a global scale despite frequent reassortment among them.
source: In contrast, influenza B viruses are currently composed of two distinct lineages (Victoria and Yamagata) (Kanegae et al., 1990; Rota et al., 1990) (Figure 1D) that diverged approximately 40 years ago and which have since co-circulated on a global scale, despite frequent reassortment among them (Chen and Holmes, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen and Holmes, 2008

claim: The HA genes of influenza B viruses exhibit lower rates of evolutionary change (nucleotide substitution) than both influenza A viruses.
source: Although the HA genes of influenza B viruses are thought to exhibit lower rates of evolutionary change (nucleotide substitution) than both influenza A viruses (Ferguson et al., 2003; Chen and Holmes, 2008; Bedford et al., 2014), their antigenic characteristics are not well understood.
evidence: Supported by citations (Ferguson et al., 2003; Chen and Holmes, 2008; Bedford et al., 2014)

claim: The antigenic characteristics of influenza B viruses are not well understood.
source: Although the HA genes of influenza B viruses are thought to exhibit lower rates of evolutionary change (nucleotide substitution) than both influenza A viruses (Ferguson et al., 2003; Chen and Holmes, 2008; Bedford et al., 2014), their antigenic characteristics are not well understood.
evidence: Statement that antigenic characteristics are not well understood

claim: Seasonal epidemic outbreaks of each influenza type are caused by the stochastic introduction of multiple virus lineages.
source: The advent of global influenza surveillance and full genome sequencing over the past decade has shown that seasonal epidemic outbreaks of each influenza type are caused by the stochastic introduction of multiple virus lineages (Nelson et al., 2008a) and that the patterns of seasonal oscillation vary between temperate and tropical regions (Rambaut et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations (Nelson et al., 2008a; Rambaut et al., 2008)

claim: The patterns of seasonal oscillation vary between temperate and tropical regions.
source: The advent of global influenza surveillance and full genome sequencing over the past decade has shown that seasonal epidemic outbreaks of each influenza type are caused by the stochastic introduction of multiple virus lineages (Nelson et al., 2008a) and that the patterns of seasonal oscillation vary between temperate and tropical regions (Rambaut et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rambaut et al., 2008

claim: The H3N2 and H1N1 subtypes of influenza A virus compete with each other resulting in the epidemic dominance of a single subtype.
source: Population genetic analysis (Rambaut et al., 2008), consistent with epidemiological data (Goldstein et al., 2011), suggests that the H3N2 and H1N1 subtypes of influenza A virus compete with each other resulting in the epidemic dominance of a single subtype.
evidence: Supported by citations (Rambaut et al., 2008; Goldstein et al., 2011)

claim: 908 full genomes of influenza B viruses were generated from over 26,000 laboratory confirmed influenza B cases sampled during 2002–2013 in eastern Australia and New Zealand.
source: To understand the evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics of influenza B virus, we generated the full genomes of 908 influenza B viruses selected from over 26,000 laboratory confirmed influenza B cases in children and adults aged from birth to 102 years sampled during 2002–2013 in eastern Australia (Queensland, n = 275; New South Wales, n = 210; and Victoria, n = 207) and New Zealand (n = 216) (Figure 2).
evidence: Describes the data collection and sequencing performed in this study, shown in Figure 2

claim: The influenza B virus strain used for vaccination did not match the dominant circulating strain during 7 of the 13 years studied.
source: Of note is that the influenza B virus strain used for vaccination in the region did not match the dominant circulating strain during 7 of the 13 years studied (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The Victoria lineage experienced strong seasonal fluctuations in relative genetic diversity.
source: Whereas the Victoria lineage experienced strong seasonal fluctuations in relative genetic diversity, little change was observed over the same time period for the Yamagata lineage, and these observations were not heavily affected by differences in sampling density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Little change in relative genetic diversity was observed for the Yamagata lineage over the sampling period.
source: Whereas the Victoria lineage experienced strong seasonal fluctuations in relative genetic diversity, little change was observed over the same time period for the Yamagata lineage, and these observations were not heavily affected by differences in sampling density (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The almost invariant relative genetic diversity of the Yamagata lineage resembled that of seasonal H1N1 viruses.
source: While the almost invariant relative genetic diversity of the Yamagata lineage resembled that of seasonal H1N1 viruses (Figure 3D), the stark and almost annual changes of diversity in the Victoria lineage were similar to those observed for H3N2 virus (Figure 3C); although H3N2 viruses exhibited a greater frequency of oscillations than those estimated for Victoria lineage viruses.
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 3D

claim: The stark and almost annual changes of diversity in the Victoria lineage were similar to those observed for H3N2 virus.
source: While the almost invariant relative genetic diversity of the Yamagata lineage resembled that of seasonal H1N1 viruses (Figure 3D), the stark and almost annual changes of diversity in the Victoria lineage were similar to those observed for H3N2 virus (Figure 3C); although H3N2 viruses exhibited a greater frequency of oscillations than those estimated for Victoria lineage viruses.
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 3C

claim: The Victoria lineage experiences strong bottlenecks between seasons similar to those described for H3N2 viruses.
source: The strong seasonal fluctuations in diversity observed for Victoria lineage suggest that this lineage experiences strong bottlenecks between seasons similar to those described for H3N2 viruses (Bedford et al., 2011; Zinder et al., 2013), whereas the almost invariant relative genetic diversity for Yamagata suggests the continuous co-circulation of multiple lineages.
evidence: Inference based on observed data patterns, supported by citations (Bedford et al., 2011; Zinder et al., 2013)

claim: The almost invariant relative genetic diversity for Yamagata suggests the continuous co-circulation of multiple lineages.
source: The strong seasonal fluctuations in diversity observed for Victoria lineage suggest that this lineage experiences strong bottlenecks between seasons similar to those described for H3N2 viruses (Bedford et al., 2011; Zinder et al., 2013), whereas the almost invariant relative genetic diversity for Yamagata suggests the continuous co-circulation of multiple lineages.
evidence: Inference based on observed data patterns

claim: The Victoria lineage was characterized by a single prominent tree 'trunk', with side branches that circulated for short periods of time (1–3 years).
source: The phylogenetic analysis of the HA genes showed that the Victoria lineage was characterized by a single prominent tree 'trunk', with side branches that circulated for short periods of time (1–3 years) (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The Victoria lineage evolutionary pattern parallels that observed for seasonal H3N2 viruses and is indicative of frequent selective bottlenecks due to the serial replacement of circulating strains.
source: This evolutionary pattern parallels that observed for seasonal H3N2 viruses and is indicative of frequent selective bottlenecks due to the serial replacement of circulating strains, as would be expected under continual antigenic drift (Grenfell et al., 2004).
evidence: Inference based on phylogenetic patterns, supported by citation (Grenfell et al., 2004)

claim: Greater diversification was observed for the Yamagata lineage, with multiple clades co-circulating for extensive periods of time.
source: In contrast, greater diversification was observed for the Yamagata lineage, with multiple clades co-circulating for extensive periods of time (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The three clades of Yamagata viruses circulating in 2013 diverged approximately 10 years ago.
source: For example, the three clades of Yamagata viruses circulating in 2013 diverged approximately 10 years ago, again paralleling the evolutionary pattern seen in seasonal H1N1 viruses.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic analysis

claim: The average time to common ancestor between contemporaneous samples fluctuated from 0 to <5 years for Victoria lineage, except during 2010 and 2011 where the genealogical diversity marginally increased to 7 years.
source: These patterns are clearly identifiable in the genealogical diversity skyline (Figure 4) in which the average time to common ancestor between contemporaneous samples fluctuated from 0 to <5 years for Victoria lineage, except during 2010 and 2011 where the genealogical diversity marginally increased to 7 years.
evidence: Supported by genealogical diversity analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The genealogical diversity of Yamagata was consistently greater and gradually increased during the sampling period.
source: In contrast, the genealogical diversity of Yamagata was consistently greater and gradually increased during the sampling period.
evidence: Supported by genealogical diversity analysis

claim: The effective reproductive number (Re) of Victoria lineage epidemics showed greater variation (median values, 1.1–1.3) between epidemics.
source: This analysis showed a greater variation in Re (median values, 1.1–1.3) between epidemics caused by the Victoria lineage, whereas the Re of Yamagata epidemics, were generally lower, varied only slightly, around 1.1 (1.08–1.14) (Figure 5A), indicating greater heterogeneity in transmission between seasons for Victoria viruses.
evidence: Supported by BDSIR model analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The Re of Yamagata epidemics were generally lower and varied only slightly, around 1.1 (1.08–1.14).
source: This analysis showed a greater variation in Re (median values, 1.1–1.3) between epidemics caused by the Victoria lineage, whereas the Re of Yamagata epidemics, were generally lower, varied only slightly, around 1.1 (1.08–1.14) (Figure 5A), indicating greater heterogeneity in transmission between seasons for Victoria viruses.
evidence: Supported by BDSIR model analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: In 2008, the median Re of 1.27 (95% HPD of 1.18–1.37) estimated for the Victoria lineage was significantly greater than that of Yamagata at 1.11 (95% HPD 1.05–1.17).
source: Both lineages transmitted with nearly equal force in 2005, whereas in 2008 the median Re of 1.27 (95% highest posterior density [HPD] of 1.18–1.37) estimated for the Victoria lineage was significantly greater than that of Yamagata at 1.11 (95% HPD 1.05–1.17).
evidence: Supported by BDSIR model analysis

claim: Victoria lineage exhibited significantly higher initial growth rate resulting in a faster epidemic with larger number of infections.
source: Analysis of the cumulative number of all influenza B positive cases through time for each season (Figure 5B) reveals significant differences in the exponential growth phase between the lineages, where Victoria lineage exhibited significantly higher initial growth rate resulting in a faster epidemic with larger number of infections.
evidence: Supported by epidemiological data analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: In 2008, the Victoria lineage exhibited a significantly faster growth rate, coinciding with the year in which a new antigenic variant of the Victoria lineage was first detected (B/Brisbane/60/2008-like viruses) in Australia and New Zealand.
source: These results also show that in 2008 the Victoria lineage exhibited a significantly faster growth rate, in correlation with the high Re, coinciding with the year in which a new antigenic variant of the Victoria lineage was first detected (B/Brisbane/60/2008-like viruses) in Australia and New Zealand.
evidence: Supported by epidemiological and phylogenetic data

claim: The B/Brisbane/60/2008-like antigenic variant emerged as the globally dominant influenza B strain in the following years and has been continuously recommended (2009–2015) as the influenza B vaccine component.
source: This antigenic variant emerged as the globally dominant influenza B strain in the following years and has been continuously recommended (2009–2015) as the influenza B vaccine component since that period in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres (Klimov et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Klimov et al., 2012) and knowledge of vaccine recommendations

claim: Combined, Australia and New Zealand were net importers of influenza viruses, except during 2002 and 2008 when the net export of the Victoria lineage was similar to the import observed during the same years.
source: Additionally, we identified that, combined, Australia and New Zealand were net importers of influenza viruses, except during 2002 and 2008 when the net export of the Victoria lineage was similar to the import observed during the same years (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by phylogeographic analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: The patterns observed for the NA and internal gene segments were similar to those observed for the HA genes.
source: These analyses showed that the patterns observed for the NA and internal gene segments were similar to those observed for the HA genes described above.
evidence: Supported by genome-wide analysis

claim: The NP genes of both lineages showed substantial differences throughout their history compared to other gene segments.
source: The single exception was the NP genes of both lineages where substantial differences occurred throughout their history.
evidence: Supported by genome-wide analysis

claim: Frequent reassortment occurred within the two lineages of influenza B virus.
source: Comparison of these phylogenies revealed frequent reassortment within the two lineages of influenza B virus (data not shown) and a few instances of reassortment between them (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic comparison of all eight genome segments shown in Figure 8

claim: During 2004, a subpopulation (approximately 15%) of Victoria-like viruses acquired all internal gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, NP, MP, and NS) from the Yamagata lineage viruses.
source: In particular, during 2004 a subpopulation (approximately 15%) of Victoria-like viruses acquired all internal gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, NP, MP, and NS) from the Yamagata lineage viruses.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis of reassortment events

claim: All remaining inter-lineage reassortment events of the Victoria HA lineages involved the acquisition of the Yamagata NP gene during 2007 and 2008, which resulted in the extinction of the previously circulating Victoria lineage NP gene.
source: Interestingly, all remaining inter-lineage reassortment events of the Victoria HA lineages involved the acquisition of the Yamagata NP gene during 2007 and 2008 (Figure 8E), which resulted in the extinction of the previously circulating Victoria lineage NP gene.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8E

claim: The only inter-lineage reassortment events for the virus carrying the Yamagata HA occurred during 2002 and 2004, when the NA and MP genes were derived from the Victoria lineage viruses, but these viruses went extinct within the same influenza season.
source: In contrast, the only inter-lineage reassortment events for the virus carrying the Yamagata HA occurred during 2002 and 2004 (red arrows in Figure 8A,F), when the NA and MP genes were derived from the Victoria lineage viruses, but these viruses went extinct within the same influenza season.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8A,F

claim: The HA gene of Victoria viruses is placed in different genetic backgrounds at a higher rate than Yamagata viruses.
source: In sum, these results show that the HA gene of Victoria viruses is placed in different genetic backgrounds at a higher rate and this is likely to have important fitness consequences.
evidence: Inference based on reassortment patterns observed in phylogenetic analysis

claim: The PB2 and PB1 gene trees exhibit deep divergence, similar to the HA gene where co-circulating viruses contain distinct Victoria and Yamagata genes.
source: Phylogenies also suggest that the PB2 and PB1 gene trees (Figure 8B,C) exhibit deep divergence, similar to the HA gene where co-circulating viruses contain distinct Victoria and Yamagata genes.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8B,C

claim: The PB2, PB1 and HA genes were consistently derived from a single lineage, except for the short-lived subpopulation in 2004.
source: Specifically, we observe that the PB2, PB1 and HA genes were consistently derived from a single lineage, except for the short-lived subpopulation in 2004.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis of reassortment patterns

claim: The HA genes of the two influenza B lineages both evolved at a rate of approximately 2.0 × 10−3 subs/site/year.
source: Despite the marked differences in their epidemiological and evolutionary dynamics, the HA genes of the two influenza B lineages both evolved at a rate of approximately 2.0 × 10−3 subs/site/year (Table 1), comparable to those previously estimated for a smaller (n = 102) global sample of influenza B viruses collected during 1989–2006 (Chen and Holmes, 2008) (mean nucleotide substitution rate of 2.15 × 10−3 subs/site/year).
evidence: Supported by molecular clock analysis shown in Table 1 and comparison with Chen and Holmes, 2008

claim: The HA substitution rates of influenza B viruses were considerably lower than those estimated for influenza A H3N2 and H1N1 viruses (5.5 × 10−3 subs/site/year, 4.0 × 10−3 subs/site/year, respectively).
source: These rates were considerably lower than those estimated for influenza A H3N2 and H1N1 viruses (5.5 × 10−3 subs/site/year, 4.0 × 10−3 subs/site/year, respectively) (Rambaut et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by comparison with rates from Rambaut et al., 2008

claim: The Victoria lineage viruses have accumulated more nonsynonymous substitutions (dN/dS = 0.19) than the Yamagata lineage (dN/dS = 0.13).
source: In contrast, analysis of the ratio of the number of nonsynonymous and synonymous substitutions per site (dN/dS) revealed significant differences between the influenza B virus lineages, with the Victoria lineage viruses having accumulated more nonsynonymous substitutions (dN/dS = 0.19) than the Yamagata lineage (dN/dS = 0.13) (p-value, <0.05).
evidence: Supported by dN/dS analysis

claim: Two amino acid residues in the Victoria HA (positions 212 and 214) experienced positive selection.
source: In addition, two amino acid residues in the Victoria HA (positions 212 and 214) were revealed to have experienced positive selection (p < 0.05), whereas no positively selected sites were observed in the Yamagata lineage over the time period studied.
evidence: Supported by positive selection analysis

claim: No positively selected sites were observed in the Yamagata lineage over the time period studied.
source: In addition, two amino acid residues in the Victoria HA (positions 212 and 214) were revealed to have experienced positive selection (p < 0.05), whereas no positively selected sites were observed in the Yamagata lineage over the time period studied.
evidence: Supported by positive selection analysis

claim: The Victoria lineage exhibited a greater dN/dS (ratio = 1.37) on internal vs external branches of the HA phylogeny compared to the Yamagata lineage (ratio = 0.98).
source: Similarly, the Victoria lineage exhibited a greater dN/dS (ratio = 1.37) on internal vs external branches of the HA phylogeny compared to the Yamagata lineage (ratio = 0.98), indicating that amino acid changes have been fixed more frequently in Victoria than Yamagata lineage viruses (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by branch-specific dN/dS analysis shown in Table 1

claim: The Victoria lineage is under greater positive selection pressure, and hence likely to experience greater antigenic drift, than the more conserved Yamagata lineage.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the Victoria lineage is under greater positive selection pressure, and hence likely to experience greater antigenic drift, than the more conserved Yamagata lineage.
evidence: Inference based on dN/dS analysis and positive selection results

claim: Victoria lineage viruses exhibited antigenic variation that generally clustered according to the year of isolation and phylogenetic distance, indicative of ongoing antigenic drift.
source: These revealed that Victoria lineage viruses exhibited antigenic variation that generally clustered according to the year of isolation and phylogenetic distance, indicative of ongoing antigenic drift, and similar to that previously reported for H3N2 viruses (Smith et al., 2004; Bedford et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by antigenic mapping analysis and comparison with H3N2 (Smith et al., 2004; Bedford et al., 2014)

claim: The antigenic distances for the Yamagata viruses had no correlation with time or phylogenetic distance and showed greater levels of antigenic cross-reactivity between antisera raised to both earlier and more recent viruses.
source: In contrast, the antigenic distances for the Yamagata viruses had no correlation with time or phylogenetic distance and showed greater levels of antigenic cross-reactivity between antisera raised to both earlier and more recent viruses.
evidence: Supported by antigenic mapping analysis

claim: The degree of antigenic distance between strains of Victoria viruses was often linked to the proximity of single amino acid substitutions to the receptor binding pocket (RBP) of the HA.
source: Structural modeling showed that the degree of antigenic distance between strains of Victoria viruses was often linked to the proximity of single amino acid substitutions to the receptor binding pocket (RBP) of the HA (Figure 9B; see structural differences section below), in agreement with recent work on H3N2 (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 9B and comparison with Koel et al., 2013

claim: The closer the amino acid change between two strains was to the RBP, the greater the antigenic difference between them.
source: Importantly, the closer the amino acid change between two strains was to the RBP, the greater the antigenic difference between them.
evidence: Inference based on structural modeling and antigenic analysis

claim: Victoria viruses infected a younger population (mean 16.8 years, median 11 years) compared to Yamagata viruses (mean 26.6 years, median 18 years).
source: On average, Victoria viruses infected a younger population (mean 16.8 years, median 11 years) compared to Yamagata viruses (mean 26.6 years, median 18 years).
evidence: Supported by epidemiological data analysis

claim: Nearly 70% of Victoria lineage viruses were identified in children <18 years, whereas the Yamagata lineage exhibited a bimodal age distribution with a significant shift toward infections in individuals aged >25 years.
source: Thus, nearly 70% of Victoria lineage viruses were identified in children <18 years, whereas the Yamagata lineage exhibited a bimodal age distribution with a significant shift toward infections in individuals aged >25 years (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by age distribution analysis shown in Figure 10

claim: These differences in age distribution are significant and unlikely to be explained by systematic bias because the same pattern was observed in both countries.
source: These differences in age distribution are significant and unlikely to be explained by systematic bias because the same pattern was observed in both countries, and are consistent with data from Guangdong, China (Tan et al., 2013), and Slovenia (Sočan et al., 2014) during the 2009–2010 and 2010–2013 epidemic seasons, respectively.
evidence: Supported by consistency across multiple countries and citations (Tan et al., 2013; Sočan et al., 2014)

claim: The higher rates of amino acid change observed in the Victoria HA were consistent with the stronger selective pressures on this viral lineage.
source: The higher rates of amino acid change observed in the Victoria HA (Figure 11A) were consistent with the stronger selective pressures on this viral lineage.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 11A

claim: All changes in the closest cluster (21 Å) to the RBP were comprised exclusively of Victoria lineage amino acid changes.
source: Notably, all changes in the closest cluster (21 Å) were comprised exclusively of Victoria lineage amino acid changes, while the few changes observed in Yamagata lineage viruses were distant to the RBP (Figure 11C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 11C

claim: Amino acid changes in both influenza B virus lineages were less frequent than those in influenza A viruses sampled over a similar time period.
source: Overall, however, amino acid changes in both influenza B virus lineages were less frequent than those in influenza A viruses sampled over a similar time period, with the H3N2 viruses showing more extensive structural change (Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparative structural analysis shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1

claim: Crystal structures showed extensive backbone differences around amino acid sites 165 and 180 that lie near the RBP between the Victoria and Yamagata lineages.
source: Notably, we also observed fundamental structural differences between the lineages (Figure 11B). Crystal structures showed extensive backbone differences around amino acid sites 165 and 180 that lie near the RBP as well as residue differences in the helix close to where α-2,3 and α-2,6 ligands differ structurally, thereby potentially influencing receptor binding (Figure 11D).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 11B,D

claim: Yamagata viruses bind predominantly to α-2,6-linked sialic acid host receptors while Victoria viruses have both α-2,3 and α-2,6 binding capacities.
source: Previous experiments suggest that Yamagata viruses bind predominantly to α-2,6-linked sialic acid host receptors while Victoria viruses have both α-2,3 and α-2,6 binding capacities (Wang et al., 2012; Velkov, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies (Wang et al., 2012; Velkov, 2013)

claim: N-glycosylation at Asn 212 occurs in both lineages but has a lower overall frequency in Victoria strains.
source: On the other hand, N-glycosylation at Asn 212 occurs in both lineages but has a lower overall frequency in Victoria strains.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis

claim: Amino acid changes in either site 212 or 214 would abolish the N-glycosylation at 212.
source: In light of the positive selection acting on codon sites 212 and 214 in the Victoria lineage, it is interesting to note that amino acid changes in either site would abolish the N-glycosylation at 212, thereby highlighting a possible functional consequence of gain or loss of a glycan at this site.
evidence: Inference based on structural and selection analysis

claim: Loss of N-glycosylation at 212 adds capacity to bind α-2,3 and not just α-2,6-linked sialic acid host receptors.
source: Furthermore, position 212 is located at the exit of the RBP which is used by α-2,3-linked sialic acid host receptors, and loss of N-glycosylation at 212 consequently adds capacity to bind α-2,3 and not just α-2,6-linked sialic acid host receptors (Figure 11E).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 11E

claim: Loss of N-glycosylation at site 212 was associated with an increased proportion in the younger (0–5 years) age group.
source: Interestingly, we observed that loss of N-glycosylation at site 212 was associated with an increased proportion in the younger (0–5 years) age group (Figure 12).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 12

claim: Subtle differences in the prevalence of α-2,3- and α-2,6-linked glycans on the cells of the respiratory tract of young children compared to adults, combined with partial changes in glycosylation patterns, could account for the observed differential age distribution of the two influenza B lineages.
source: We therefore hypothesize that subtle differences in the prevalence of α-2,3- and α-2,6-linked glycans on the cells of the respiratory tract of young children compared to adults (Nicholls et al., 2007; Walther et al., 2013), combined with partial changes in glycosylation patterns, could account for the observed differential age distribution of the two influenza B lineages.
evidence: Hypothesis based on structural and epidemiological observations, supported by citations (Nicholls et al., 2007; Walther et al., 2013)

claim: The Victoria lineage experiences strong bottlenecks between seasons due to periodic selective sweeps.
source: The strong seasonal fluctuations in diversity observed for Victoria lineage suggest that this lineage experiences strong bottlenecks between seasons similar to those described for H3N2 viruses (Bedford et al., 2011; Zinder et al., 2013), whereas the almost invariant relative genetic diversity for Yamagata suggests the continuous co-circulation of multiple lineages.
evidence: Inference from observed patterns of genetic diversity fluctuations

claim: The higher Re of the Victoria viruses reduces the mean age of infection.
source: One possible explanation is that the higher Re of the Victoria viruses reduces the mean age of infection, as expected in the case of a disease like influenza that imparts some immunity following infection (Anderson and May, 1992).
evidence: Hypothesis based on epidemiological theory, supported by citation (Anderson and May, 1992)

claim: The relatively older population is better protected against Victoria virus because of a broader immune response.
source: Alternatively, the inability of Victoria viruses to infect an equivalent proportion of other age groups may mean that the relatively older population is better protected against this virus because of a broader immune response.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed age distribution patterns

claim: The mean age of infection for the B/Brisbane/60/2008-like antigenic variant of the Victoria lineage increased from 15 years (median, 12) in 2008 to 20.5 years (median, 14) in 2011, which coincided with a gradual drop in Re from its peak in 2008.
source: The former scenario is supported by an increase in the mean age of infection from 15 years (median, 12) in 2008 to 20.5 years (median, 14) in 2011 for the B/Brisbane/60/2008-like antigenic variant of the Victoria lineage, which coincided with a gradual drop in Re from its peak in 2008 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by epidemiological data analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The phylodynamic pattern of the Victoria lineage HA gene is indicative of a virus population under greater selection pressure that escapes host immunity by accruing beneficial amino acid substitutions in the HA gene.
source: In particular, we find significant differences in the evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics between the Victoria and Yamagata lineages (Table 3). Central to this is the observation that the phylodynamic pattern of the Victoria lineage HA gene is indicative of a virus population under greater selection pressure that escapes host immunity by accruing beneficial amino acid substitutions in the HA gene.
evidence: Inference based on phylodynamic analysis and selection pressure data

claim: The highest rate of viral adaptation occurs at intermediate levels of immune pressure.
source: Indeed, theory predicts that the highest rate of viral adaptation occurs at intermediate levels of immune pressure (Grenfell et al., 2004) which may characterize the Victoria lineage.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work (Grenfell et al., 2004)

claim: The Victoria lineage evolutionary pattern ensures that there is a constant supply of susceptible individuals—both naïve and reinfected individuals which in turn increases Re.
source: Such an evolutionary pattern ensures that there is a constant supply of susceptible individuals for Victoria lineage viruses—both naïve and reinfected individuals which in turn increases Re—which then exhibit a pattern of genomic diversity and lineage turnover that is significantly faster and more periodic than Yamagata lineage viruses.
evidence: Inference based on evolutionary and epidemiological patterns

claim: The Yamagata viruses are under weaker immune selection pressure and accordingly experience weaker antigenic drift.
source: In contrast, the phylodynamic patterns exhibited by Yamagata viruses are indicative of a virus population that exhibits slower and less periodic dynamics, reflected in a lower and more consistent Re, in turn suggesting that these viruses are under weaker immune selection pressure and accordingly experience weaker antigenic drift.
evidence: Inference based on phylodynamic analysis

claim: Clinical trials of influenza B virus vaccination in children and experimental infection of mice showed that the Yamagata antigens produced a stronger immune response than the Victoria antigens.
source: Interestingly, clinical trials of influenza B virus vaccination in children (Skowronski et al., 2011) and experimental infection of mice (Skowronski et al., 2012) showed that the Yamagata antigens produced a stronger immune response than the Victoria antigens.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies (Skowronski et al., 2011; Skowronski et al., 2012)

claim: If natural infection with influenza B virus was similar to vaccination, this would imply that Yamagata viruses are less able to evolve through antigenic drift and therefore escape the immune response.
source: If natural infection with influenza B virus was similar, this would imply that Yamagata viruses are less able to evolve through antigenic drift and therefore escape the immune response (Grenfell et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculative inference based on vaccination studies, supported by citation (Grenfell et al., 2004)

claim: These fundamental differences in evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics are driven by differences in hemagglutinin binding preferences.
source: We propose that these fundamental differences in evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics are driven by differences in hemagglutinin binding preferences.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings

claim: The respiratory tissue of children mainly have α-2,3-linked receptors with a lower level of α-2,6-linked receptors than adults.
source: Experimental studies in children (aged up to 7) (Nicholls et al., 2007) and adults have shown that the respiratory tissue of children mainly have α-2,3-linked receptors with a lower level of α-2,6-linked receptors than adults, and these differences among the different age groups may in part account for the different age distribution of the two B lineages.
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study (Nicholls et al., 2007)

claim: The greater propensity to infect children will increase Re, initiating the epidemiological and evolutionary pattern that characterizes the Victoria lineage.
source: In turn, the greater propensity to infect children will increase Re, initiating the epidemiological and evolutionary pattern that characterizes the Victoria lineage.
evidence: Inference based on epidemiological and structural findings

claim: Given sufficient coverage, Yamagata viruses might experience a major drop in prevalence over time through targeted control methods, such as the extensive use of quadrivalent influenza vaccines containing both B lineages.
source: As a consequence, there is a greater chance that, given sufficient coverage, Yamagata viruses might experience a major drop in prevalence over time through targeted control methods, such as the extensive use of quadrivalent influenza vaccines containing both B lineages, in contrast to the more adaptable Victoria viruses.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on observed evolutionary and epidemiological patterns
